title: High Frequency Storm Sampling and Analysis of Hysteretic Transport Behavior Offers Insights Into Dynamic Microplastic Activation, Flux and Depletion Within a Peri‐Urban Stream
content:
Abstract

Previous research has pinpointed storm events as significant potential controls of microplastic (MP) export to the oceans. Hysteretic behavior of discharge (Q)—concentration (c) relationships for suspended sediment (SS) and solutes has been found important in understanding the dynamic activation and transport of these substances, additionally providing better estimations of long-term loads. Due to limited availability of high frequency event-based MP concentration data their potential hysteretic behavior has not been studied, leaving a substantial knowledge gap regarding the fate and transport mechanisms controlling MP activation and retention within catchments. We pioneer the use of high frequency MP data collected during a storm event revealing the time variable activation of different sources and transport mechanisms within a peri-urban catchment. Surface water samples were collected before, during and after the event and combined with discharge and turbidity data to quantify MP concentrations and fluxes. Analysis of the hysteretic behavior of the Q-c relationship revealed a clockwise hysteresis pattern with MP concentration peaking before Q, suggesting potential MP supply limitation for the sampled event. Regression analysis indicates Q to be the primary driving force promoting MP flux, with strong correlations between Q and MP concentration in rising and falling limbs. A strong Q - turbidity relationship was observed only in the rising limb, potentially indicating spatial differences in the sources of SS and MPs transported in the falling limb. Total MP flux increased by 17–217 times to that of baseflow, highlighting the significance of often-overlooked dynamics when calculating yearly MP flux.
